chapters.title: Brit: Cutting a Covenant
chapters.subtitle: In Hebrew you don’t make a covenant — you cut one, in blood.
chapters.trueMeaning: A life-and-death bond sealed in blood
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew phrase for making a covenant is *karat brit*, “to cut a covenant,” because ancient covenants were sealed by cutting animals and walking between the pieces. In Genesis 15 God alone walks the bloody path while Abraham sleeps, taking the whole weight of the promise on Himself. The chapter sees this as the gospel in advance: in Jesus, God cuts a new covenant in His own blood, so it rests on His faithfulness, not ours.
chapters.bigIdea: A biblical covenant is not a contract but a one-sided, blood-sealed pledge of God’s love that He alone guarantees.

So our security rests on Christ, not our consistency

sections.h: You Don’t Make a Covenant — You Cut One
p: In English we “make” agreements. In Hebrew you **cut** a covenant. The phrase is *karat brit*. *Karat* means to cut off, sever or amputate; *brit* means covenant, alliance or sacred pact. Put together, the words paint a raw picture: flesh cut open, blood poured out, two lives tied together.

That is why the Jewish ceremony of circumcision is called *brit milah*, the “covenant of circumcision.” It is a literal cut in the flesh that marks a boy as part of the covenant God made with Abraham.

English still has a faint echo of this in the phrase “to cut a deal,” but in ancient Israel the idea was deadly serious. A covenant was a bond of life and death, sealed in blood. Breaking it meant calling destruction down on your own head.

Yet the chapter stresses that *brit* was never mainly about fear. It was about **faithfulness**. God did not need anything from His creatures, so His covenants were not business deals. They came out of love.

sections.h: The Night God Cut a Covenant with Abraham
p: Genesis 15 shows this most clearly. God had already promised Abraham children, land and blessing. Now He tells Abraham to seal those promises in a covenant ceremony. Abraham cuts a heifer, a ram and a goat in half (the birds are left whole) and lays the halves in two rows with a path down the middle.

This looks strange to us, but it was normal in the ancient Near East. Both partners walked between the dead animals together, as if saying: “Let this happen to me if I break my word.” It was a walk of death that guaranteed life.

Then comes the surprise. Abraham falls into a deep sleep and a thick darkness comes over him. **Only God passes between the pieces**, appearing as a smoking firepot and a blazing torch. Abraham promises nothing; he just watches. The covenant is **unilateral** — one-sided. God alone carries it and God alone will fulfil it.
And since God is eternal and cannot die, a promise backed by His life cannot fail. In effect God is saying: I will keep My word and give you the blessing, even if it costs Me My life.
> It is the gospel before the cross.

sections.h: Why Would a King Bind Himself to a Peasant?
p: Ancient covenants were usually between a strong king and a weaker “vassal” (a subject ruler). The king promised protection, food and peace; the vassal promised loyalty and tribute, often a tax. But what could the King of the universe possibly gain from creatures made of dust?

**Nothing — and that is the point.** God’s covenants are acts of humble, stooping love. He does not cut them to get something from us; He cuts them because He wants *us*. With Abraham He is not hiring a servant but adopting a son: “You are Mine, I am yours, and My life is pledged to you even if you have nothing to give back.”
So Abraham’s only part was to **believe**. He did not walk the path or sign a contract. He trusted the God who promised, and God counted that trust as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

Much modern religion pictures God as conditional: He blesses when we obey and punishes when we fail. Covenant turns that picture upside down. In *brit*, God is not using our obedience as leverage; He is offering Himself.

He does not say, “Measure up and I’ll love you.” He says, “I love you. Walk with Me and live.” The chapter puts it this way: covenant is not a cage but a commitment, not a leash but a lifeline. When God binds Himself to people, He is not tightening His grip — He is opening His heart.

sections.h: Jesus: The New Covenant in His Blood
p: At the Last Supper Jesus lifts a cup of wine and says, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20). The chapter hears an echo of Genesis 15. This time the covenant is not cut with animals but in Jesus’ own body. Once again God walks the path of blood, not humanity; He carries the promise, not us.

That is why the New Testament calls the New Covenant “better”: it is sealed not with the blood of bulls but with the blood of God Himself. Hebrews 9:12 says Christ entered the holy place once for all by His own blood, securing **eternal** redemption — not a temporary patch.

The chapter insists on the order: Jesus did not die *so that* God could love us; He died *because* God already did. The New Covenant is the ultimate *brit* — a bond no sin can break, no failure can undo, and no power can cancel.

For people who worry that their flaws will cut them off from God, covenant is the answer. The New Covenant does not depend on how consistent you are; it depends on Christ’s blood. You may stumble or doubt, but God cut the covenant alone. Your job is not to earn it but to trust it, as Abraham did.

That kind of covenant brings deep, steady peace. It shows that God is not only Creator but Partner, not only Sovereign but faithful, not only holy but bound to us in blood. The God who walked between the pieces in Abraham’s vision is the same God who walked up Calvary — and the blood that once marked an altar now marks a cross. He pledged His life to our redemption, and He will never break His word.

chapters.title: Ezer: Helper — Much More Than Just a Server
chapters.subtitle: The word used for Eve is the word the Bible most often uses for God.
chapters.trueMeaning: Strong rescuer who supplies what’s lacking
chapters.nutshell: Genesis 2:18 calls the woman an *ezer*, a “helper,” and some have read that as a servant created to obey men. But in the Hebrew Bible *ezer* most often describes God Himself, the strong one who rescues the weak. The chapter argues that the word speaks of honour, strength and completion, and points to a vision of mutual submission and Christlike, serving leadership.
chapters.bigIdea: An ezer is not a subordinate assistant but a strong helper who supplies what is missing — the same word the Bible uses for God.
skeleton: Eden is a love story: relationship before sin
‘Helper’ has been misread as ‘servant’
Ezer mostly describes God, the stronger rescuer
Adam was incomplete; Eve brings different strengths
The New Testament model is mutual submission
Leadership means Christlike, self-giving service
Male and female together reflect God’s image
We, too, are called to be helpers like God

p: Many people read the Garden of Eden only as the story of sin, shame and separation. The chapter invites a different lens: it is a **love story** — between Adam and Eve, and between God and humanity. God walks in the garden, clothes the naked, and calls out to people even when they hide. He looks less like a furious judge and more like a grieving parent or faithful lover.

The whole Bible, read this way, is a divine romance in which God pursues His people. And it starts with relationship, not wrath. Before there is sin there is aloneness, and before there is a fall there is a helper.

Genesis 2:18 says: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper (*ezer*) suitable for him.” Centuries of debate hang on this one word. Is the woman a lower servant, or a sacred support?

In some conservative and fundamentalist circles, this verse is used to teach that women were made to serve men — obedient, silent assistants. One popular author even states flatly that Scripture says God created woman to serve man.

But that is not what the Hebrew says or how it feels. *Ezer* means helper, yes, but **not** in a small or inferior sense. Think about it: who usually needs help, the weak or the strong? The weaker one. And whom do they turn to? Not someone even weaker, but someone **stronger** or more able. That is what makes the word “helper” so significant.

sections.h: Ezer Is a Word for God
p: Trace *ezer* through the Old Testament and you find something surprising: it **most often describes God Himself**. Psalm 70:5 cries, “I am poor and needy; come quickly to me, O God. You are my *ezer* and my deliverer.” Psalm 33:20 says, “We wait in hope for the LORD; He is our *ezer* and our shield.”

This is not a master calling a servant; it is a desperate person crying for rescue. Again and again *ezer* names the one who saves, holds up and strengthens. If *ezer* meant inferior, then God would be inferior to us — which is absurd.
> A helper is not weaker. A helper is often the stronger one.

We look for help when something is missing — perspective, wisdom, support or strength. That is why we go to doctors, counsellors, lawyers and friends. Calling someone a helper admits we cannot do it alone. It is a place of **honour**, not lower rank.

So when God says Adam needs an *ezer*, He is not saying Adam needs an assistant. He is saying **Adam is incomplete**. And God does not give him another man or a copy of himself, but someone like him and yet wonderfully different — flesh of his flesh, with her own gifts, intuition and glory.

Women may usually have less raw physical strength, but that is only one kind of power. The chapter notes that women often excel in emotional intelligence, social awareness, resilience and intuition. In many marriages husbands look to their wives not for obedience but for wisdom, grounding and insight. That, too, is *ezer*.

The Bible acknowledges structure but never celebrates inequality; it undermines domination. The New Testament pattern for relationships is not command-and-control but **mutual submission**. Ephesians 5:21 says, “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” — and that command introduces the very passage often used to argue that wives must submit to husbands. The point is honour, not a pecking order.

The chapter grants that every human institution needs someone with the final word — a president, a general, a CEO. But real greatness in leadership comes from using authority to **serve** with wisdom, humility and responsibility.

Jesus defined authority by sacrifice: “Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15:13). In John 13 He wraps a towel around His waist and washes His disciples’ feet. So if a man leads, let him lead like Christ; and if the woman is his *ezer*, let her help with strength, grace and no shame.

In the end *ezer* is not just a word for women; it is a word for God — our help, rescue and strength in weakness. In making the woman an *ezer*, God was not assigning inferiority; He was giving Adam what only God can give: **wholeness**. When we call God our *ezer* we worship Him, so when Eve is called *ezer* we should honour her.

Notice too that Genesis says it is not good for man to be *alone*, not merely *lonely*. Loneliness is a feeling; aloneness is a condition. God is not just meeting Adam’s emotional needs but completing a picture: **male and female together reflect God’s image**, and neither is enough alone.

Eve is not an afterthought but the finale of creation, after which God declares everything “very good.” Together the man and woman are not master and servant but partners in purpose, co-heirs of the garden and stewards of creation.

When we are weak, afraid or failing, we cry out, “Help me! Save me!” God answers not with a shout from far above but with His **presence**. He never shames us for needing help; He becomes our help. “You are my help (*ezer*) and my deliverer; you are my God, do not delay” (Psalm 40:17).

This is the heartbeat of *ezer*: love that shows up, strength that meets us where we lack, presence that holds us up without dominating. The chapter calls readers to honour helpers as reflections of God’s own help — and to become helpers themselves. When we help, we do what God does: fill what is missing, mend what is broken and bring wholeness.

chapters.title: Kadosh: Holy — The God Who Comes Close
chapters.subtitle: Holiness isn’t God flinching from sin; it’s God being utterly different — and coming near.
chapters.nutshell: A popular saying claims “God is too holy to look upon sin.” The chapter answers that the Hebrew *kadosh* means set apart, unique and dedicated — the opposite of common, not a fragile allergy to imperfection. Scripture shows God seeking out sinners again and again, and Jesus, the Holy One, eating with them; true holiness moves toward the mess to heal it.
chapters.bigIdea: God’s holiness is His unique, set-apart love that draws near to sinners to heal them, not a purity that makes Him look away.
skeleton: Claim: God is too holy to look at sin
Kadosh means set apart, the opposite of common
Holy days, objects and people are dedicated, not sinless
Scripture shows God engaging sinners again and again
Jesus embodies holiness by touching and eating with sinners
God loves sinners; He does not hate them
Purity laws protect life, like an operating room
Holiness can’t look away — it steps in to heal

p: Many people have heard that “God is too holy to look upon sin.” The idea comes from Calvinist theology and is widespread in Protestant churches, especially fundamentalist ones. A prominent Reformed writer even described the cross by saying the Father could not bear to look at His Son and had to turn away His eyes.

That may sound devout, but the chapter says it misreads both the Bible and the Hebrew idea of holiness. *Kadosh*, usually translated “holy,” does **not** mainly mean “morally spotless and unable to stand imperfection.” It means **set apart, unique, distinct**.
Yes, God is without sin. But when Scripture calls God *kadosh*, it is stressing how different and one-of-a-kind He is — not that He is delicate or easily upset by human failure.

We usually think holy is the opposite of sinful. In Hebrew thought holy is closer to the **opposite of common**. To be holy is to be consecrated — dedicated to a higher purpose. This can apply to God, to places, to people, and even to time. “Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you” (Exodus 31:14).

When God made the seventh day holy, He was not calling the other six days evil; He was setting one day apart for a special purpose. Likewise, the Temple utensils were holy not because they were sinless (they were objects!) but because they were reserved for God’s use.

A biblical scholar sums it up: the basic meaning of the word is “consecrated” or “devoted,” and it expresses **commitment** within covenant relationships. So calling God holy means He is unlike anyone else — His love, justice, mercy, power and patience are all in a class of their own. As Hosea 11:9 puts it, “I am God, and not a man — the Holy One among you.”

sections.h: Can a Holy God Look at Sin?
p: If *kadosh* meant God cannot be near sin, we would have a serious problem: sin is everywhere, so God would have to stay far from the world He made, the people He loves, and His own rescue mission.

But Scripture tells another story. After Adam and Eve sin, God walks in the garden and **seeks them out**. In Job 1 Satan himself comes before God and God talks with him. In the wilderness God lives right in the middle of sinful Israel — the tent of meeting “is among them in the midst of their uncleanness” (Leviticus 16:16).

If God could not look at sin, how could He love and speak with David (an adulterer and murderer), Moses (who killed a man), Peter (who denied Jesus three times) or Paul (who persecuted the church)? The answer is that God’s holiness is **not fragile** — it is transforming. Our sin does not damage God; it damages us.

The clearest picture of God’s holiness is not His distance from sinners but His **presence among them**. Jesus, “the Holy One of God,” sat, ate, touched and blessed sinners. Matthew 9:10 notes that many tax collectors and sinners ate with Him at Matthew’s house.

If holiness meant avoiding contamination, Jesus failed badly. But if holiness means bringing something unique and different into broken places, Jesus is *kadosh* perfectly. He did not make people clean up first; His touch made them clean. He touched the leper, welcomed outcasts, healed on the Sabbath and wept with the grieving.

In Luke 15 the father runs to the returning prodigal and dresses him not in shame but in a robe of honour. And 2 Corinthians 5:21 goes further still: God made the sinless one “to be sin for us,” so that we might become God’s righteousness in Him.

sections.h: The God Who Moves Toward the Mess
p: The whole sweep of Scripture contradicts the idea that God cannot look at sin. God does not turn away; He rolls up His sleeves and enters the story. Paul told the Athenians, “In Him we live and move and have our being… we are His offspring” (Acts 17:28).

Contrast that with a well-known modern Calvinist pastor who insists that God really does hate sinners, not just sin. The chapter disagrees strongly: God loves people **while they are still sinners** (Romans 5:8). He draws near and seeks out the broken.

God did not make us immortal, all-knowing or flawless like Himself. He made us fragile, limited and slow to understand. So His judgment is not cold; it is full of mercy from a Creator who remembers we are dust. The Incarnation is not a loophole in God’s intolerance but the clearest expression of His love — like Jesus longing to gather Jerusalem’s children “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matthew 23:37).

In Leviticus *kadosh* appears nearly 100 times and “impurity” around 130 times, yet neither is mainly about moral evil. Impurity was often connected with death, disease or disorder. The goal was not to punish but to **purify** — to make room again for God to live among His people.

The chapter offers an analogy: holiness is like an **operating room**. It is not “holy” because it is too angry to look at germs. It is kept clean because it is a place of healing. If it gets contaminated, it is cleaned — not because the surgeon is furious, but because lives are at stake.

So God’s presence in the Tabernacle was not fragile but fierce, and its purity rules existed to protect and preserve life, not to shut people out. Now, through Jesus, that holiness lives inside believers: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Saying God is too holy to look at you in your sin misses the whole point. Holiness is not divine disgust but **divine distinction** — a love that cannot be polluted, yet chooses to step into pollution to heal it.

Jesus did not flinch from sin; He carried it. He did not run from the cross; He embraced it. He did not wait for us to get it right; He came while we were still sinners. That is *kadosh*: not separation from sinners, but their redemption; not distance from darkness, but light breaking into it.
> The gospel isn’t about a God who can’t look at us — it’s about a God who can’t look away.

The chapter closes with a picture of a compassionate Father running to embrace the prodigal and saying, “Be holy, as I am holy” — meaning nearness, love and likeness, not separation. He is not ashamed to be called our God, and He is not too holy to look you in the eye.

chapters.title: Shachah: Worship — Even Without Music
chapters.subtitle: Biblical worship is bowing low and offering something costly, not a mood set by music.
chapters.trueMeaning: Bowing low and offering something costly
chapters.nutshell: Today “worship” often means a music night. The Hebrew *shachah* means to bow down or lie face-down, and in the Bible worship was always tied to sacrifice — bringing your best to God. The chapter argues that Jesus redefined that sacrifice as costly love for people, so true worship is seen in serving the poor, the stranger and the enemy.
chapters.bigIdea: Worship is a surrendered life that offers something costly to God, now expressed mainly through sacrificial love for others.
skeleton: Modern worship = music and atmosphere
Shachah = bowing low before someone greater
Ancient worship always involved a costly offering
Cain and Abel: the heart and quality matter
After the Temple, worship drifted from deeds to words
Jesus redefined sacrifice as serving ‘the least of these’
Praise celebrates; worship surrenders and sacrifices
Worship in spirit and truth: actions match words

p: Say “worship night” and many modern Christians picture a dim room, loud music, raised hands and a worship leader guiding the crowd through big choruses. It feels spiritual and sounds beautiful. But is that what the Bible means by worship? Not exactly.

The Hebrew word is *shachah*: to **bow down**, kneel or lie face-down. It is not about atmosphere or great music; it is about the heart’s posture and a life of surrender. In its oldest form, worship meant lowering yourself before someone greater and **offering something costly**. You could not worship without making a sacrifice.

Praise might be sung, but worship was *done*. You never came to Israel’s God empty-handed. You brought your best lamb, your first fruits, your finest oil. Something died; something was given. Worship was not a music genre — it was an **offering**.

In the ancient Near East, people came to their gods with food — in effect, a meal for the deity. The smell of roasting meat rose from altars as a “pleasing aroma.” This was not because God was hungry, but because **love gives**; love sacrifices. People believed that if they wanted divine protection, provision or presence, they had to bring something — and something good.

Genesis 4 shows the pattern. Abel brought “fat portions from the firstborn of his flock” — the ancient equivalent of top-grade wagyu beef. Cain brought “some of the fruits,” perhaps produce that was already going bad. God was pleased with one and not the other. The chapter argues the issue was not blood versus plants but **quality**: Abel gave his best, Cain gave leftovers.

That sets the tone for all worship: what matters is the heart behind the gift. To *shachah* is to lower yourself and lift up something valuable to God — bowing your pride, your time and your comfort before someone worthy.

When the Temple was destroyed (AD 70), animal sacrifices stopped. The Pharisees reshaped Jewish worship to be word-based rather than deed-based, replacing the altar with **prayer**. Over time Christians absorbed the same shift: worship became songs and lyrics. Action was replaced with words.

But Jesus never dropped the idea of sacrificial worship — He **redefined** it. In Matthew 25:35–40 He says: I was hungry and you fed me, thirsty and you gave me a drink… whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.

This is the altar of the New Covenant: not stone but flesh, not incense but service. Worship now happens in sacrificial love and relationships — in alleys, prisons, shelters and on the margins. Want to worship God? Feed the hungry, clothe the cold, love your enemy. That is *shachah*.

The apostles urged believers to become **living sacrifices** (Romans 12:1). This was more than a figure of speech; it was a call to pour out your life as Christ poured out His. Jesus did not worship mainly with songs but with His body — with sweat, tears and blood.

To worship like Jesus is to carry your cross daily, weep with those who weep, give when no one is watching and love when no one deserves it. Here, the chapter says, Western worship culture often misses the mark: we confuse **emotion with devotion**. If the music moves us, we assume God is pleased. But worship is not about what we feel; it is about what we offer.

Hebrews 13:16 says, “Do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” God is not moved by our playlists but by our compassion — especially when we give our best to someone who can give us nothing back.

Music is not the problem. Psalm 150 calls for praising God with trumpet, harp, lyre and cymbals. But **praise and worship are not the same thing**. Praise is celebration. Worship is surrender and sacrifice.

Singing is beautiful, but *shachah* happens when we kneel beside a homeless man and give him dignity, open our homes to strangers, forgive the unforgivable, love the unlovable and give without expecting anything back. James 1:27 calls pure religion caring for orphans and widows in their distress. That kind of worship, the chapter says, “smells like heaven” — a fragrant offering that delights God.

Jesus told the Samaritan woman at the well that true worshippers worship “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23). The chapter explains: **spirit** means no masks, no performance; **truth** means alignment — our actions matching our words. God wants authenticity, faith that travels from the heart to the hands.

You can sing about justice and still ignore the poor; you can declare God’s worth and still live selfishly. That is not worship; it is noise. Through Amos God says, “I hate your festivals… but let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:21, 24). The prophets knew what many have forgotten: God is not impressed by holy spaces filled with empty songs. He wants hearts that bend low and hands that reach out.

The chapter invites us to imagine a worship night with no stage, only a soup kitchen; no stage lights, only streetlamps as coats are handed to people in the cold; no guitar, just shared laughter and restored dignity. That is *shachah* — not because it lacks beauty or reverence, but because it **embodies** them in the most down-to-earth way.

“If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person?” (1 John 3:17). Worship is not a lifestyle accessory but a cross-shaped posture, a poured-out life.
So before planning a worship night, ask: Will this cost us anything? Will it touch the hungry, broken and lost? Will it bow low and lift someone else up?
> Shachah is not about the volume of our voices — it’s about the weight of our love.

chapters.title: Sane: Hate — To Avoid, Reject and Ignore
chapters.subtitle: Biblical ‘hate’ is turning away, not boiling rage.
chapters.trueMeaning: To reject, avoid, turn away from
chapters.nutshell: In modern English “hate” means burning hostility, but the Hebrew *sane* mostly means to reject, avoid or not choose — like stepping around a thorn. Read this way, “Esau I hated” means “I did not choose Esau,” and Jesus’ call to “hate” family means “choose Me first.” The chapter argues that preachers who use Psalm 5:5 to claim God hates all sinners misread both the word and its context: God turns from evil but loves and longs for sinners.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical hate is rejection and distance, not rage — so God turning from evil never means He stops loving sinners.
skeleton: English ‘hate’ = emotional hostility
Hebrew sane = reject, avoid, turn away (thorn seed)
‘Esau I hated’ = I did not choose him
‘Hate your family’ = choose Jesus first

In context Psalm 5 rejects idolaters and false gods
Hate is the absence of blessing, like darkness or cold
God is love: He rejects evil but longs for sinners

p: In today’s English, “hate” is a hot, emotional word. It suggests hostility, disgust, loathing — even wanting to hurt someone. Saying you hate someone usually means fury or personal grudge, and the word is linked with violence and deep wounds.

The Hebrew word translated “hate,” *sane*, works very differently. It is broader, more practical and much less emotional. It often means **to reject, avoid, ignore or turn away from**. It describes distance more than anger — what happens when someone is no longer chosen or welcomed, but set aside or left behind.

A standard lexicon of ancient Hebrew (a dictionary of word origins) traces *sane* to old picture-letters: a **thorn** and a **seed**, together “thorn seed.” Just as you swerve to avoid stepping on a thorn, to *sane* someone is to turn aside from them — to avoid or reject them.

sections.h: Hate as Rejection: Jacob and Esau
p: In Romans 9:10–13 Paul quotes Malachi 1: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (*sane*).” In context this is not God wishing Esau harm or torment. It is about **election** — God choosing. God chose Jacob, not Esau; He set Esau aside in favour of Jacob. Here “hate” simply means “I did not choose him.”

Paul uses the same Hebrew idea in Ephesians 5:29: “No one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for it.” A modern reader might object, “But I hate my nose!” Paul, though, means that to *sane* your body would be to **ignore** it. Nobody really does that: we feed it, give it water, clothe it, and respond when it needs the toilet. We don’t reject or abandon it.

This also explains one of Jesus’ hardest sayings: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters — yes, even their own life — such a person cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

To modern ears this sounds awful. How could the Prince of Peace tell us to hate our families? But Jesus was a Jewish teacher speaking in Hebrew categories. He was not commanding emotional hostility. He meant: **choose Me over them**. Be willing to walk away, if it ever comes to that, in order to follow Me.

For many Jewish followers of Jesus this is very real: when relatives beg them to give up their faith, they must decide between family expectations and Christ. Saying no to that pressure is not hating their family in the modern sense — it is exactly what Jesus meant by *sane*.

sections.h: Does God Hate Sinners? The Misuse of Psalm 5:5
p: Some influential Reformed preachers say Psalm 5:5–6 proves God hates sinners: “You hate all who do wrong; you destroy those who tell lies; the bloodthirsty and deceitful you, LORD, detest.” From this a number of well-known modern pastors and writers have built a disturbing theology: that God is furious with people and loathes them until they accept Christ.

Their statements are blunt. One famous theologian called “God hates the sin but loves the sinner” nonsense and said God finds us loathsome and cannot stand to look at us. A popular preacher taught that humanity is “a hateful thing” that deserves to be hated. A leader at a major Reformed network said the cross implies God hates humans. Another prominent pastor said God does hate sinners, citing Psalm 5; another preached that God hates not just what you do but who you are.

Their reasoning runs roughly like this: (1) people who sin are sinners; (2) everyone sins; (3) God hates sin; (4) therefore God hates everyone. The chapter calls this a complete misreading of both the language and the heart of Scripture — built on English translations and on reading modern meanings back into ancient words.

Scholars point to a different background. A leading Hebrew scholar describes Psalm 5 as a **rejection of false gods** by someone accused of idolatry. An Old Testament professor explains that the psalm shows Israel’s God setting Himself apart from pagan gods, who were thought to contain both good and evil; Israel’s God revealed that evil exists apart from Him.

So a better summary than “God hates us all” is that **God rejects and turns away from idol worship**. The “evildoers” of Psalm 5 are not ordinary people who sometimes slip up, but those who worship false gods and commit horrors such as child sacrifice.
> It is not a hatred of humanity. It is a rejection of wicked systems, cultures and spiritual rebellion.

sections.h: Hate as the Absence of Blessing
p: The chapter suggests thinking of *sane* like darkness or cold. Darkness is not a thing; it is the **absence** of light. Cold is the absence of heat. In the same way, biblical hate is the absence of connection, blessing, affection and involvement.

That is why anger and hate are not the same. When you love someone, you get angry at their self-destruction — you argue, grieve and step in. When you “hate” someone biblically, you go quiet, keep away and let go. Picture a wife who hates her husband: she is not the one shouting; she is the one who has quietly packed her bags and left. She has disengaged.

sections.h: God Turns from Evil but Loves Sinners
p: So when Scripture says God “hates” evildoers, it means He turns away from their destructive ways, removes His protection and resists them. It does **not** mean He stops loving them.

Jesus was God in the flesh, and He touched the unclean, ate with sinners, forgave prostitutes and wept over murderers. If God hated sinners the way some Calvinist preachers claim, Jesus could not be God. But He is — and He loved sinners. “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Paul even calls himself the worst of sinners whom Christ came to save (1 Timothy 1:15). If God hated all sinners in the fundamentalist sense, Paul could never have been saved.

This error paints God as a raging tyrant instead of a loving Father. But God is not rage; **God is love** (1 John 4:8). Yes, He disciplines and judges, but His aim is always redemption, never punishment for its own sake. He withholds blessing from the wicked to call them back, not to crush them in disgust.

Jesus told us to love our enemies so that we may be children of our Father in heaven (Matthew 5:44–45). Children copy their father — so if we must love enemies, it is because **our Father loves enemies too**.

God “hates” evil because He is love and cannot take part in it, so He distances Himself from it. But distance is not indifference. In the parable of the prodigal son, the father sees his son “while he was still a long way off” and runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20). It was the father himself, not a servant, who spotted him — as if he had been watching the road every day, hoping. He did not hate his wayward son; he longed for him.

Our Father does not punch sinners in the face; He dies for them. He does not hate the world; He so loved it. The chapter urges readers to reject the abusive idea that God loathes people and return to a God who loves, a Saviour who embraces and a Spirit who draws near.

chapters.title: Naqam: The Vengeance That Heals
chapters.subtitle: God’s ‘vengeance’ is justice that sets things right, not payback.
chapters.nutshell: Modern “vengeance” means getting even. The Hebrew *naqam* is about setting things right — rebalancing the scales that evil has tipped — and Scripture links God’s vengeance with comfort, purification and repentance. Because only God’s justice can heal, we are told to leave vengeance to Him, forgive, and overcome evil with good.
chapters.bigIdea: God’s vengeance is restorative justice that rescues and purifies, which is why we leave it to Him and answer wrong with mercy.
skeleton: Western vengeance = emotional payback
Naqam = setting right, rebalancing the scales
Human revenge soothes ego; God’s justice heals
God’s day of vengeance comes with comfort
His wrath refines like fire; it aims at repentance
So we leave room for God and forgive
Love must judge; Jesus bore justice to give mercy
Our task: resist retaliation, trust God

p: In Western culture “vengeance” tastes of rage and retaliation. We think of film anti-heroes, bloody justice and explosive payback — settling the score in a brutal, personal way. When the Hebrew Bible speaks of vengeance, it invites a different picture, driven not by ego or pain but by **restorative justice** and God’s long-term mercy.

*Naqam*, usually translated “vengeance,” means more than retaliation. It points to **setting things right** — a divine act rooted in faithful covenant justice rather than angry punishment. Its core idea is not destruction but corrective rebalancing: bringing balance back where evil and injustice have tipped the scales.

When people seek revenge, bruised egos and unhealed pain usually lead the way. Revenge is rarely about justice; it is about feeling better and soothing wounded pride. Nations go to war, families split and reputations are wrecked in the name of “justice,” when really it is **pain demanding to be seen**.

God’s vengeance is not like that. Scripture presents His wrath not as chaotic fury but as focused, purposeful and redemptive — **justice that heals**. Isaiah 61:2 announces “the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, to comfort all who mourn.”

Notice that vengeance and comfort appear in the same breath. God’s vengeance is not for entertainment or ego; it is to comfort mourners and free the broken-hearted from what sin has done. It is His passionate justice rushing in to rescue what evil tried to destroy.

Paul echoes this in Romans 12:19: “Do not take revenge… but leave room for God’s wrath, for it is written: ‘It is mine to avenge; I will repay,’ says the Lord.” Why step back? Not because God’s payback will be harsher, but because His vengeance can achieve something ours cannot: **restoration**.

Human vengeance only knows how to punish; divine vengeance knows how to **purify**. We judge from pain; God judges from love. Isaiah 1:24–26 shows this: God vents His wrath on His foes, then says He will purge away the dross (impurities in metal), restore Jerusalem’s leaders, and afterwards it will be called “the City of Righteousness.”
> God’s wrath is like a refining fire, not a wildfire that destroys.

The prophets keep reminding us that God’s judgment aims at renewal. Even His most dramatic acts — like the plagues on Egypt — were designed for repentance, not mere destruction. Yes, the Nile turned to blood and Egypt shook. But hearts were stirred, and Egyptians as well as Israelites left in the Exodus (“a mixed multitude,” Exodus 12:38).

God’s “vengeance” cracked Pharaoh’s empire so the light of deliverance could break through for everyone who believed. It was not an explosion of fury but an **invitation to salvation**. In the same way, the judgments in Revelation call the nations to turn and be healed. Even at the end of history, God’s justice carries one last merciful call: come home.

Retaliation is the natural, fleshly response; forgiveness is divine. When we take justice into our own hands, we just keep the pain going — the person who hits back guarantees the next blow. When we choose mercy and give up revenge, we make room for God to step in and **transform both** the wrongdoer and us.

“Bless those who persecute you… Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:14, 21). We are not called to be agents of God’s punishment but reflections of His heart. Forgiveness does not pretend the wrong never happened. It says: I will not be the one to repay, and I will not let your sin turn me into someone I’m not.
Jesus, the embodiment of divine justice, did not cry for revenge from the cross. He said, “Father, forgive them.”

sections.h: Restorative Judgment and a Love That Judges
p: A good judge in a healthy society does not hand out punishments to feel better. He discerns the truth, weighs the circumstances and seeks justice that leads to restoration. In God’s way of doing things vengeance is never the last word — **redemption is**. “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).
Even God’s wrath carries this longing: not to destroy but to wake people up, not to shame but to heal. God exposes sin the way a doctor exposes a wound — so it can finally be treated.

People sometimes mean “God is love” in a soft, harmless way. But love that never says no, never corrects and never protects is not love. **Love must judge.** Divine judgment is what happens when God’s love collides with human injustice — not the opposite of grace, but grace in action.

When Jesus cleared the Temple courts, it was not temper but love reaching its limit with injustice; He overturned tables to cleanse, not destroy. And in the greatest act of divine “vengeance,” Jesus took the full weight of sin on Himself — not to crush the world but to redeem it. He bore justice to give us mercy.

Living in the spirit of *naqam* means resisting retaliation and **entrusting justice to God**. It means speaking truth without turning bitter, seeking justice without losing mercy, refusing to repay evil with evil, and trusting God to deal with those who hurt us — even when it takes longer than we would like.

Above all, our response to wrong should reflect God’s instinct for redemption, not the world’s instinct for revenge. “Vengeance is mine,” says the Lord — not because He is angrier than we are, but because He is wiser, purer and more committed to saving the world.
So when someone wounds you, pray instead of striking back. When wronged, forgive instead of retaliating. When mistreated, let go instead of plotting revenge — and let God be God.

chapters.title: Shevet: The Rod That Guides, Not Strikes
chapters.subtitle: The ‘rod’ in Proverbs is a shepherd’s staff, not a weapon for beating children.
chapters.nutshell: Proverbs 13:24 (“whoever spares the rod hates their children”) has been used to justify beating children, most notoriously by a best-selling Christian parenting manual. The chapter shows that *shevet* is a shepherd’s staff used to protect, guide and inspect sheep — never to beat them — and that the abuse grows from a picture of God as a violent Father. Biblical discipline means teaching and leading with care, as the Good Shepherd does.
chapters.bigIdea: The biblical rod is the shepherd’s tool of loving guidance and protection, so ‘discipline’ means teaching, not hitting.
skeleton: Proverbs 13:24 weaponised to justify beating children
Shevet is a shepherd’s staff, not a weapon

Abusive ‘discipline’ leaves real, tragic damage
‘Careful to discipline’ and ‘train’ mean teach and guide
The rod of iron means unbreakable shepherding rule

sections.h: A Verse Turned into a Weapon
p: Few verses have been misused as badly as Proverbs 13:24: “Whoever spares the rod (*shevet*) hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them.” Many read it not as parenting wisdom but as God’s approval of **corporal punishment** (hitting as punishment). In some teachers’ hands, the “rod” has become a licence for cruelty.

The chapter’s main example is a best-selling Christian parenting manual written by a Baptist preacher and his wife. It has sold over a million copies in dozens of languages and tells parents to “discipline” children with belts, plastic tubing, whips and switches, even cold showers and withholding food. It presents spanking, whipping and “breaking the child’s will” as biblical love, and even claims a child’s conscience *demands* a whipping to remove guilt.

This theology of fear and pain leans heavily on one word, *shevet*. The chapter calls the interpretation not only wrong but spiritually toxic — and sometimes deadly. Several children have died from abuse inspired by the book, and others have grown up damaged, angry and afraid, convinced that love looks like pain. But what if *shevet* was never meant to strike?

In Hebrew *shevet* does not mean a weapon; it is a **shepherd’s staff**. Israel was, and still is, a land of shepherds — even today you can see Bedouin herding sheep beside modern highways. A shepherd’s rod was never made for beating sheep. It was a tool of guidance, defence and authority, with three main jobs:
**Protection** — driving off predators. **Direction** — gently blocking a sheep that starts to wander. **Inspection** — counting the flock and checking each sheep’s health.

So the rod symbolises presence, care and loving authority — not punishment. That is why David, Israel’s most famous shepherd, wrote: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod (*shevet*) and your staff, they **comfort** me” (Psalm 23:4).
> Comfort. Not fear. Not bruises. Not broken wills.

How did *shevet* end up justifying abuse? It began with translation — not just of words, but of worldview. The Western world inherited a lens shaped more by **Roman punishment and Calvinist guilt** than by Hebrew covenant love. Through that lens discipline came to mean pain, authority came to mean domination, and the shepherd’s rod became an instrument of wrath.

Add a version of the gospel in which an angry Father must pour out His wrath on His Son to satisfy His justice, and it is easy to see how earthly fathers came to believe that love means pain, that physical punishment redeems, and that God “beats” His children into submission.

But that is not the God of Scripture, nor the Jesus who took children in His arms, blessed them and said, “Let the little children come to me.” The problem is not Proverbs 13; it is a framework that pictures God as abusive.

sections.h: The Rod Turned Against the Sheep
p: A shepherd does not beat his sheep or frighten them. Panicked sheep simply bolt and stampede the rest of the flock. Sheep must be handled with extra gentleness — not with whips, belts, plastic tubes, switches or rods.

The only time a shepherd struck with his rod was in **defence**, to fight off wolves or thieves. Tragically, some teachers have turned the rod away from the predators and onto the sheep themselves. The chapter calls this reversal not just tragic but demonic.

Children are not wolves to be beaten but **lambs to be led**. A child’s spirit is soft and shapeable, not something to be “broken” like a wild horse. Love builds rather than bruises; discipline instructs rather than injures. When a child is harmed in God’s name, it is God’s name that is dishonoured.

The chapter describes real cases from a fundamentalist religious community in Israel where these methods were followed. One sincere family “trained up” their three sons by the book — flogged, isolated and “broken.” One son later died by suicide, another went to prison, and the third became homeless and addicted, and then died.

Another pastor beat his children to force obedience; both sons became drug addicts unable to keep jobs or relationships. The son of yet another pastor, after a lifetime of physical abuse at home, beat his own wife to death in 2023 — while his father still believed he had acted in love, just as he imagined God the Father did at the cross.

The chapter insists these are not rare exceptions but the fruit of theology gone wrong. When the cross is seen as an act of divine violence rather than self-giving love, parenting becomes fear-based, and children grow up terrified of mistakes and cut off from grace.

Look again at Proverbs 13:24. The second half says the loving parent is **careful** to discipline. That describes attentiveness, wisdom and consistency — not rage, reaction or abuse. The key word is *care*, not *corporal*.

Proverbs 22:6 says, “Train up a child in the way they should go, and when they are old they will not depart from it.” “Train” here means to dedicate — to build pathways, shape character and build trust through faithfulness, not through fear and pain.
And when Jesus came, He did not whip children into shape. He blessed them and held them up as the model of the kingdom: “Unless you become like one of these…” (Matthew 18:3).

The English word *discipline* shares its root with *disciple*. To discipline is to **teach**, not to terrorise — to help a child become who they were meant to be, training them in love rather than punishing them into compliance.
Good discipline teaches responsibility, not fear. It leads toward maturity, not mere submission. It creates safety, not silence.

sections.h: Shevet as Rule, Not a Club
p: Psalm 2 says the Messiah will “rule the nations with a rod of iron.” The word is again *shevet*, but the image is not a bludgeon. It pictures **unshakable authority** and leadership that cannot be corrupted: iron, unlike wood, was seen as unbreakable. It is the rod of justice, not the stick of punishment.

Revelation 12 repeats the phrase about the Messiah born from Israel, and the Greek verb used is *poimainō* — **to shepherd**. So this rod is not a club but a shepherd’s staff: righteous leadership and unyielding protection. The rod was never about pain; it was always about presence.

sections.h: Healing the Wounds: Shepherd, Not Slave Master
p: Many people raised in fear-based homes, where love was confused with control, limp spiritually for life. Some run from God entirely; others stay stuck in performance-based religion, always trying to earn love or dodge punishment. The gospel offers a better Father — one who guides rather than strikes, disciplines out of mercy rather than anger, and mends hearts rather than breaking wills.

Research into the family backgrounds of serial killers and abusers points to a sobering pattern: hyper-legalistic parenting that wounds body and soul is one of the surest ways to breed criminal behaviour. When discipline becomes domination and rules replace relationship, the damage can run deep and turn violent.

How we picture our heavenly Father — tender and compassionate, or angry and hateful — shapes how we raise our children. If people see the cross as a Father abusing and killing His Son, it is no surprise when they justify abusing their own children as “godly discipline,” afraid that if they don’t hit hard enough, God will.

But God is a Good Shepherd who leads us beside still waters and restores our soul; His rod comforts rather than bruises. To truly train up a child is to walk with them, not whip them; to correct in love, not crush with power; to give them the same mercy God gave you — using our hands not to hurt, but to heal.

verses.text: Whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them.
I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
Train up a child in the way they should go, and when they are old they will not depart from it.
You will rule them with a rod of iron.
Unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

keyPoints: Proverbs 13:24 has been weaponised to justify beating children, with tragic results.
Shevet is a shepherd’s staff used to protect, direct and inspect sheep — and it brings comfort.
A Western lens of Roman punishment, Calvinist guilt and an angry-Father view of the cross turned the rod into rage.
Shepherds struck predators, never the sheep; children are lambs to be led, not wolves to be beaten.
‘Careful to discipline’ and ‘train up’ point to attentive teaching, not violence.
Discipline comes from the same root as disciple: it means teaching.
The Messiah’s ‘rod of iron’ means unbreakable, shepherding authority (Greek poimainō).
reflect: How has your picture of God as Father shaped the way you think about discipline?
What is the difference between correcting someone and crushing them?
If you lead others (siblings, teams, future children), how could you use your ‘rod’ like a shepherd?

quiz.q: What is a shevet in its original setting?
quiz.why: It was the shepherd’s tool of guidance, defence and authority.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three main uses of the shepherd’s rod listed in the chapter?
quiz.why: The rod struck only predators, never the sheep.

quiz.q: In Psalm 23:4, what does the rod and staff do?
quiz.why: ‘Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.’

quiz.q: What Greek verb does Revelation use for ruling ‘with a rod of iron’?
quiz.why: The rod of iron is a shepherd’s staff of unbreakable leadership.

Physical punishment, such as hitting or spanking.
Greek verb meaning to shepherd, used in Revelation for the Messiah’s rule.
From the same root as disciple: teaching and training, not inflicting pain.
